heading: DHŪ AL-KIFL (AS)
title: THE BEAUTY OF PATIENCE AND RIGHTEOUSNESS
themes: Steadfastness • Righteousness • Keeping Trust • Patient Action • Humility • Mercy • Responsible Promises
scope: 8 CONNECTED STORIES | 12 INTERACTIVE MISSIONS | 3 PRIMARY QUR’ANIC VERSES
introduction: Volume Twenty continues the ʿIBRAH Junior journey after al-Yasaʿ (AS), whose name appeared beside Dhū al-Kifl in Ṣād 38:48. The Qur’an explicitly mentions Dhū al-Kifl in two places: al-Anbiyāʾ 21:85 and Ṣād 38:48. The following verse, al-Anbiyāʾ 21:86, praises the people named collectively as righteous and recipients of Allah’s mercy. The Qur’an does not give Dhū al-Kifl a detailed childhood, a known city, a narrated trial, a named family member or specific dialogue. We will not manufacture those details.

Many classical scholars regarded Dhū al-Kifl as a Prophet because he is included with the Prophets, while other commentators described him as an honoured righteous servant; Ibn Kathīr explicitly records the disagreement. For educational continuity, this series includes Dhū al-Kifl among the honoured figures studied in the Prophets curriculum, but never presents the disputed classification as an uncontested Qur’anic statement. The most secure Qur’anic descriptions are patient, righteous and excellent.

stories.title: The Name Beside al-Yasaʿ
stories.subtitle: A few certain words are greater than a hundred guesses

blocks.text: The school exhibition had ended, but its green-and-gold display board remained in Sheikh Uncle’s library. Imaan was carefully removing the last paper leaves when Akhlaq found a blank square beside the name al-Yasaʿ. A narrow strip of paper had been pinned underneath it: ṢĀD 38:48. “Another story is hiding here!” Akhlaq exclaimed. “Perhaps we shall find a whole book of adventures.”

Sheikh Uncle handed him a Qur’an. The verse named Ismāʿīl, al-Yasaʿ and Dhū al-Kifl, describing them as among the excellent. Then Dadi Jaan opened al-Anbiyāʾ 21:85–86. There, Dhū al-Kifl appeared with Ismāʿīl and Idrīs, and Allah praised them for patience and righteousness. Akhlaq opened his notebook to draw an ancient palace. “But which palace did he live in?” he asked. “The Qur’an does not tell us,” said Dadi. “Then I shall draw a giant mountain.” “It does not tell us that either,” Imaan answered.

Sir Zameer, preparing a new learning day at the academy, had written a sign: STEADY HANDS, TRUE PROMISES. He asked the children to make a source folder with four headings: Qur’an, classical explanation, general guidance and our own fiction. Akhlaq disliked having so many blank lines. “We could fill them with exciting guesses,” he proposed.

“Or,” Sheikh Uncle said, “we could show that truth has value even when it is brief. Scholars have discussed whether Dhū al-Kifl was a Prophet or an honoured righteous servant. We should explain that discussion fairly, not pretend a verse says what it does not.”

By evening the new board had only three Qur’anic references. Akhlaq looked at them again and realised they were not empty. They contained three large ideas: patience, righteousness and excellence. He wrote beneath them: A SHORT TRUE ACCOUNT IS BETTER THAN A LONG INVENTED ONE.
The children agreed that their next learning day would be about practising those qualities in the world they actually lived in. The next morning, their first test would arrive before the school bell.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Honour a short true source rather than filling gaps with invented history.

stories.title: The Day the Plan Changed
stories.subtitle: Patience can include disappointment and practical action

blocks.text: Rain struck the academy windows just as Team Amanah carried its boxes into the courtyard. The children had prepared a community reading morning with colourful seating mats and a table of donated books. Mohsin stood with his arms full of posters and watched the first drops turn into a downpour. “Everything is ruined,” he said. Akhlaq kicked a loose pebble. “We worked for days!”

Sir Zameer checked the slippery path. “No one is going outside until it is safe,” he announced. The children wanted an immediate solution. Imaan suggested moving the event inside, but the library was already crowded. Mohsina looked at the attendance list and noticed several younger pupils who would arrive with grandparents. “We cannot simply cancel without telling people,” she said.

Dadi Jaan had visited the classroom to deliver a box of bookmarks. She saw their disappointed faces and did not demand that they smile. “It is all right to be upset,” she said. “Patience is not pretending that a problem does not exist. You may tell a trusted adult how you feel, then ask what safe action is possible.”

Akhlaq remembered the verse naming Dhū al-Kifl among the patient. “Did something like this happen to him?” he asked. “The Qur’an does not report such an event,” replied Dadi. “We are taking a general lesson about ṣabr into our own school problem. We must keep that difference clear.”

With the teachers’ permission, they made three decisions. The event would move to the following afternoon; families would receive clear messages; and anyone who could not attend could borrow a small book bundle later. Mohsin helped dry the posters. Akhlaq called the families with Sir Zameer nearby. Imaan checked that the temporary boxes did not block an emergency exit.

The storm continued, but the children’s work now had direction. “I still feel sad about today,” Akhlaq admitted. “You may,” said Dadi. “Patience does not erase sadness. It helps us respond well while sadness is present.”
On a new card Akhlaq wrote: STOP. ASK FOR HELP. CHOOSE THE NEXT RIGHT STEP. He would need that card very soon.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Patience permits feelings, help-seeking and sensible action.

stories.title: The Queue at the Library Door
stories.subtitle: Waiting patiently while noticing other people

blocks.text: The next afternoon the rain had gone, and the reading event finally began. Its smallest visitors entered first. Soon a long queue formed at the borrowing desk, where Mohsina was placing simple labels on each book. Akhlaq stood near the front clutching a book about ocean animals. “We have been here forever,” he groaned. A younger child beside him looked close to tears.

Akhlaq considered pushing toward the table, but Imaan saw an older visitor leaning on a walking stick. She quietly asked the supervising teacher whether a chair could be brought. Mohsin moved a spare chair into a safe place, and Mohsina explained the queue to new arrivals. The teacher organised a separate assistance desk so nobody had to stand longer than necessary.

“What about my book?” Akhlaq whispered. “It is still there,” Imaan replied. “But look at the people around us.” Akhlaq frowned. He had thought patience meant merely waiting while his own frustration grew. Now he could see that good waiting also meant not making someone else’s turn harder.

A small boy dropped three paper slips. Akhlaq helped gather them and showed him where to return them. He did not give away a queue position that belonged to someone else, and he did not pretend to be in charge of the event. He asked the teacher before changing any arrangements. When the boy smiled, Akhlaq began to feel less trapped by the waiting.

Later Sheikh Uncle reminded the children that the Qur’an praises patience in al-Anbiyāʾ 21:85, while other verses teach justice and caring conduct. “We should not say we know how Dhū al-Kifl waited in a line,” he added. “This is your own small practice.”

At last it was Akhlaq’s turn. He chose the ocean book and then noticed that the little boy had taken a much thinner book. “Would you like me to read the first page with you?” he asked. The boy nodded.
In his notebook that night, Akhlaq wrote: PATIENCE HAS ROOM FOR OTHER PEOPLE. Underneath he added a quiet question: Could a promise also be part of patience?

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Waiting well includes noticing and protecting others.

stories.title: A Promise Written Too Quickly
stories.subtitle: Good intentions still need an honest plan

blocks.text: The academy received a request from a nearby family centre: could the children prepare thirty welcome packs for a weekend visit? Each pack would hold a reading card, a pencil and a short note. Before anyone checked the supplies, Akhlaq waved his hand. “Yes! We can make one hundred!” He loved the sound of a grand promise.

Sir Zameer thanked him for his enthusiasm but did not write the number down. “First count what we have, then ask what time and help are available,” he said. Mohsina counted twenty-four pencils. Imaan found thirty-five reading cards. Mohsin could help for one hour before his family appointment. The group also needed approval for printing. One hundred packs would be impossible that week.

Akhlaq felt that reducing the number would make him appear less generous. “But I meant to help,” he protested. “You did,” Sir Zameer replied, “and that matters. Yet other people may plan around your words. It is kinder to promise what you can responsibly deliver than to offer a grand number you cannot fulfil.”

At home, Salaam read a general Qur’anic reminder from al-Isrāʾ 17:34 about fulfilling commitments. Then he carefully distinguished it from Dhū al-Kifl’s brief Qur’anic mention. “Classical reports sometimes discuss responsibilities associated with his name,” he said, “but this verse about promises is teaching us a general duty. We are not claiming to know a specific promise Dhū al-Kifl made.”

The children telephoned the centre with their teacher. They agreed to make twenty packs on time, with the possibility of more only if additional supplies arrived. Akhlaq hesitated before speaking, then said clearly: “We can commit to twenty. We will update you if that changes.”

They prepared a checklist and assigned fair, manageable tasks. Imaan arranged the notes. Mohsina checked each pack. Mohsin stacked them carefully. Akhlaq labelled the boxes and checked that every pencil was present.

The next morning, the centre confirmed that twenty was a helpful number. Akhlaq realised that a small fulfilled promise could be more useful than a large impressive announcement. He wrote a new card: COUNT FIRST. COMMIT CLEARLY. REPORT HONESTLY.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: A modest promise fulfilled is better than an impressive promise abandoned.

stories.title: The Missing Team Box
stories.subtitle: A trust cannot be protected by hiding a mistake

blocks.text: Two days before the visit, the blue box holding the completed welcome packs disappeared from the storage shelf. Akhlaq had been the last child to carry it. When Sir Zameer asked where it was, Akhlaq suddenly felt hot. “It must have been moved by someone else,” he said, although he was not sure.

Imaan noticed his hesitation. “We should not accuse anyone,” she whispered. “We need to find out.” Together they told Sir Zameer exactly what they knew: Akhlaq had carried the box from the classroom; the storage shelf was empty; no one had checked the office. They walked with the teacher to the office and found the box behind a chair, where Akhlaq had placed it to keep the doorway clear.

“I forgot,” he said. “I was afraid you would all be angry.” Sir Zameer did not laugh at him. “Mistakes happen. False certainty makes them harder to fix. When something entrusted to you goes missing, report the facts, ask for help and correct the problem.”

Later the children discussed a general verse from al-Nisāʾ 4:58 about returning trusts to their owners. Dadi Jaan explained that a trust can be a physical thing, a task, a promise or information that must be handled responsibly. She also reminded them that the Qur’an calls the group including Dhū al-Kifl righteous, but gives no story about a lost box or an entrusted object in his life.

Mohsina proposed an easy check-in system. Whoever moved a box would write its location on the classroom board. Mohsin suggested two people verify the final packs before delivery. Akhlaq volunteered for the first shift, but Sir Zameer reminded him not to accept more duties than he could manage. Responsibility also meant recognising limits.

At the end of the day the box was ready in its proper place. Akhlaq approached his friends. “I am sorry I spoke as if someone else moved it. I had forgotten.” They accepted the apology and helped him finish the checklist.
He added one more line to the promise card: WHEN I MAKE A MISTAKE, TELL THE TRUTH SO WE CAN REPAIR IT.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Protect a trust with clear facts and honest correction.

stories.title: A Difficult Apology
stories.subtitle: Self-control with safety and a fresh start

blocks.text: The final posters were being arranged when a disagreement broke out. Mohsin believed that his drawing had been removed from the exhibition without permission. He raised his voice at Akhlaq. “You always decide everything!” Akhlaq shouted back, “That is not true!” Within moments both boys were talking so loudly that the younger children stopped reading.

Sir Zameer brought them to a quieter corner and asked each child to explain one fact at a time. The drawing had been moved to a different board by an adult who was making space for an accessible path. Nobody had thrown it away. Mohsin felt embarrassed. Akhlaq still felt hurt by the accusation. Sir Zameer listened to both without demanding an immediate smile.

When they had calmed down, Sheikh Uncle spoke about the Qur’an’s praise of the patient. “Does being patient mean never becoming angry?” Akhlaq asked. “No,” he answered. “It means learning not to let anger push you into wrong action. You can pause, seek help and speak truthfully. If someone is unsafe or hurt, getting help comes first.”

Mohsin looked at Akhlaq. “I should not have accused you before checking. I am sorry.” Akhlaq replied, “I am sorry for shouting. I could have explained without shouting.” Neither boy had to pretend the words had not hurt. They agreed to use the teacher’s help if another disagreement became too heated.
That afternoon Mohsina handed them a two-sided card. One side said PAUSE BEFORE REACTING. The other said REPAIR WHAT YOU CAN. “It is a practical reminder,” she said, “not a magical charm.”

The boys helped move the drawing to a visible place where the walkway stayed clear. There was no trophy for saying sorry. The benefit was simpler: the work could continue, and no child had to carry an unfair accusation.
Before leaving, Imaan asked a question that surprised everyone: “What if someone tries their best and still does not receive thanks?” Sheikh Uncle smiled. “That is a useful question for tomorrow.”

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Self-control means pausing, seeking help and repairing harm.

stories.title: No Trophy for Helping
stories.subtitle: Righteousness is not a public competition

blocks.text: On the morning of the community event, Team Amanah discovered that several tables still needed wiping and the small chairs were stacked unevenly. Every volunteer preferred the welcoming desk, where visitors would see their badges and thank them. No one wanted the quiet work at the back.

Akhlaq looked at the unused cloths. He thought about the praise in al-Anbiyāʾ 21:86: the people mentioned were among the righteous and were admitted into Allah’s mercy. “Could we have a scoreboard to show who is most righteous?” he asked, only half joking.

Salamah, who had joined the volunteers, shook her head. “We can count the packs we deliver and the tables we clean. We cannot measure who is most beloved to Allah or what is hidden in someone’s heart. The Qur’an honours the people it names; a school app cannot assign that honour.”

Imaan chose to help organise the chairs. Mohsina carefully checked that the doorway remained wide enough. Mohsin offered to carry the light boxes, while adults handled anything too heavy. Akhlaq took a cloth and began wiping the tables. Soon the room was comfortable for visitors, though nobody had watched every small task.

A younger pupil later asked whether helping quietly was pointless if nobody noticed. Dadi Jaan replied, “Goodness is not made worthless because people fail to applaud. But if you are carrying too much or need help, you should ask. We do not teach children to exhaust themselves to prove sincerity.”

When the welcome packs were delivered, the family centre thanked the whole group. Sir Zameer praised the completed responsibilities without ranking the children’s faith. He asked each volunteer to name one useful action someone else had done. Akhlaq mentioned Mohsina’s careful arrangement of the doorway. Mohsina thanked him for the neatly prepared tables.

The learning-day board now had three cards beneath Dhū al-Kifl’s name: PATIENCE. RIGHTEOUSNESS. EXCELLENCE. Beside them were ordinary photographs of boxes and books, not images of a Prophet. Akhlaq realised that the cards did not describe their own spiritual status. They reminded them to keep learning and trying.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Practice goodness without pretending to measure hearts.

stories.title: The Card We Will Keep
stories.subtitle: A small truthful promise for the days ahead

blocks.text: The exhibition ended without fireworks or prizes. When the visitors left, Team Amanah gathered in the library to put every book and chair back in its proper place. The old family-tree poster from their previous journey hung on the wall beside the new Qur’anic source folder. Imaan traced the sequence of names they had studied: Ibrāhīm, Ismāʿīl, Isḥāq, Yaʿqūb and the many others who followed in their learning journey.

Akhlaq opened his notebook to the page for Dhū al-Kifl. He had expected the volume to contain a dramatic palace, a journey through distant lands and a famous speech. Instead, it contained three Qur’anic verses, a careful explanation of what scholars discussed, and a week of small choices at school. “Is that enough to call this an important world?” he asked.

Sheikh Uncle placed the notebook beside the Qur’an. “What Allah has told us is worthy of remembrance. We should not make up more because we want every lesson to look like an adventure. The adventure for you and Imaan is learning how to behave when life gives you an actual choice.”

Each child chose one practice to carry forward. Mohsin decided to check facts before accusing anyone. Mohsina chose to make safe spaces for younger visitors. Imaan chose to listen patiently when someone needed help. Akhlaq paused. He wanted to promise that he would never make another mistake. Then he remembered the welcome packs.

“I cannot promise that,” he said. “But I can promise to tell the truth when I make a mistake and ask for help to put it right.” Salaam smiled. “That is a promise you can work to keep.” Salamah reminded everyone that learning continues even after a difficult day. A missed action was an opportunity to restart, not a reason for shame.

Dadi Jaan placed a final card beside the source folder. On it were two questions: WHAT DID ALLAH REVEAL? WHAT GOOD CAN I PRACTISE TODAY? Underneath she wrote: OUR NEXT WORLD BEGINS WITH A CALL IN DARKNESS.
Akhlaq looked up. “Is that the story of Prophet Yūnus?” Dadi smiled. “In shāʾ Allāh. But carry these lessons with you first: patience, truth and responsible action.”

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Remember revelation accurately and keep one achievable character commitment.

missions.question: A friend asks you to describe Dhū al-Kifl’s palace for the learning board.

choices.text: Explain what the verse says and leave unknown details blank.
choices.feedback: Accuracy shows respect for revealed knowledge.

choices.text: Draw a palace and label it as a certain historical fact.
choices.feedback: An attractive drawing cannot turn an unsupported claim into a revealed fact. Review the evidence and try again; do not deduct faith points or shame the learner.

choices.text: Tell the friend there is no reason to learn this name.
choices.feedback: A brief Qur’anic mention is still meaningful and worthy of study. Review the evidence and try again; do not deduct faith points or shame the learner.

choices.text: Insist the Qur’an states every later historical detail.

choices.text: Explain the verse itself and the attributed scholarly disagreement calmly.
choices.feedback: Respectful attribution preserves clarity while allowing scholarly difference.

choices.text: Call both classmates ignorant and stop the conversation.
choices.feedback: Disagreement can be discussed without insulting the people who are learning. Review the evidence and try again; do not deduct faith points or shame the learner.

synthesis.text: What the Qur’an establishes

In al-Anbiyāʾ 21:85, Allah names Dhū al-Kifl with Ismāʿīl and Idrīs and says all were among the patient. The next verse, 21:86, says Allah admitted the group into His mercy and that they were among the righteous. Ṣād 38:48 names Dhū al-Kifl with Ismāʿīl and al-Yasaʿ and describes them as among the excellent. Those descriptions are our certain historical foundation. The Qur’an does not give us episodes through which we may reconstruct Dhū al-Kifl’s day-to-day life. Classical scholarship discusses both the status of Prophethood and several traditions, which must be attributed and evaluated, not presented as revelation.
The eight lasting lessons
Respect the exact words Allah revealed; do not fill historical gaps with made-up scenes.
Patience can involve disappointment, prayer, adult support and constructive choices.
Steadfastness should protect others’ dignity rather than silence the vulnerable.
Offer promises within your real ability, then communicate if circumstances change.
Treat entrusted things and information carefully; ask for help when a mistake occurs.
Speak truthfully when angry and repair unfair words.
Do useful work without competing to prove whose faith is greater.
Keep one small, voluntary character practice going after the lesson ends.
Seven-day family character practice
Day
One achievable action
Private Muḥāsabah prompt
Read al-Anbiyāʾ 21:85 with a caregiver.
What did the verse clearly say?
Try “pause, ask, act” during a minor disappointment.
Did I seek help if I needed it?
Show kindness while waiting or taking turns.
Did I respect another person’s place?
Make one realistic promise and write down the plan.
Did I check what I could actually do?
Return one entrusted object or report its location.
Was I truthful about a mistake?
Use a calm fact-checking sentence during a misunderstanding.
Did I protect someone’s dignity?
Review 21:85–86 and 38:48 and select a next-week practice.
What do I want to keep improving?
Final knowledge and character assessment

Knowledge checks: correctly identify the two places naming Dhū al-Kifl; explain the significance of 21:86 as a continuation; recognise patience, righteousness and excellence; distinguish the Qur’an from a reported Tafsīr tradition; state that the Prophet/righteous-servant classification has classical disagreement. The educational assessment tests source comprehension, not a child’s private spiritual condition.

Character application: choose a safe response when plans change, when a promise becomes unrealistic, when entrusted property is missing, and when someone makes an unfair accusation. Encourage children to explain why their response protects truth and dignity. Do not require them to disclose personal conflicts or distress.

Family discussion: “What can we say with certainty about Dhū al-Kifl?” “Which stories must not be invented?” “How is patience different from unsafe silence?” “What will I do when I cannot complete a promise?” “Can I help without receiving a trophy?”
FINAL CARRY FORWARD • Patient faith is not a performance. Remember Allah’s guidance truthfully, fulfil responsibilities with care, and make the next right choice.
